blocks.content: Every package you've ever ordered comes with a tracking number. That one code follows it through the warehouse, onto a truck, through a sorting facility, and finally to your door. You don't need five different tracking numbers for five different steps. One code, handed to anyone along the way, tells you exactly where things stand.

A correlation id is the same idea, borrowed for backend systems. A single user request in a real microservices setup can bounce through five, ten, even twenty different services before it's done. Without something like a tracking number, finding out what happened to one specific request is close to impossible.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351813-105070128.png
blocks.alt: A single tracking number follows a package through a warehouse, a truck, and a delivery

blocks.content: A correlation id is the tracking number for a request instead of a package.
1. Introduction

Picture a checkout request in a typical microservices backend. It hits an API gateway, then a cart service, then an inventory service to reserve stock, then a payment service to charge the card, maybe a notification service after that. Five separate processes, five separate log files, maybe five separate machines.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351813-866380688.png
blocks.alt: Cart, inventory, and payment services each keep their own logs with nothing tying them together

blocks.content: Now say the payment step fails for one specific customer at 2:47 PM. Every service logged something around that time, for hundreds of other requests too. Nothing in any of those lines says which one belongs to which request. You're stuck grepping for a rough timestamp and a customer name, hoping you get lucky.

blocks.title: Even a good log aggregator can't save you here
blocks.content: Piping everything into Datadog or an ELK stack helps you search faster, but it still needs a shared field to filter on. Without a correlation id, you're eyeballing timestamps no matter how nice the dashboard looks.
2. The core idea

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple. Generate one unique id at the very edge of the system, usually the API gateway or whichever service touches the request first, and pass that same id along with every single call made because of it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352635-729711234.png
blocks.alt: The API gateway generates a correlation id the moment a request arrives

blocks.content: Every service that touches the request downstream includes that same id in every log line it writes. Cart logs it. Inventory logs it. Payment logs it. Nobody generates a new one partway through, the id is set once and just rides along for the whole trip.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352636-116986809.png
blocks.alt: The same correlation id rides along as a request moves from cart to inventory to payment

blocks.content: ["Unique per request, not per user or per session","Generated once, at the earliest point the request enters your system","Immutable, it never changes as the request hops between services","Everywhere, it shows up in every log line any service writes while handling that request"]
items: Unique per request, not per user or per session
Generated once, at the earliest point the request enters your system
Immutable, it never changes as the request hops between services
Everywhere, it shows up in every log line any service writes while handling that request

blocks.content: 2.1 What makes a good id

It doesn't need to mean anything. A random UUID works fine, some string of hex characters nobody will ever read by eye. The only real requirements are that it's unique enough to never collide with another request, and cheap enough to generate that doing it on every single request isn't a concern.
2.2 Generated once, at the edge

One detail trips people up early. The id gets generated once, by whichever service sees the request first, not regenerated by every service that touches it afterward. If the payment service made up its own new id instead of reusing the one it received, you'd be back to disconnected ids and none of this would work. Downstream services extract and forward, they don't generate, unless somehow no id was present at all.
3. How propagation works

In practice the id travels as an HTTP header. Two names are common, X-Correlation-ID and X-Request-ID, and plenty of companies just pick one and standardize internally. Whichever name you choose, every service in the chain has to agree on the same one or the whole scheme quietly breaks.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352637-396515341.png
blocks.alt: A service reads the incoming id, writes it into its own log lines, then forwards it unchanged

blocks.content: Each service does three things with the header. It reads the id off the incoming request. It attaches that id to every log line it writes while handling the request. And it forwards the id unchanged on any outgoing call it makes because of that request. That last part matters as much as the first two, forgetting to forward the header on an outgoing call is the single most common way this pattern breaks in practice.
3.1 Synchronous calls
For a normal service to service HTTP call, forwarding the header is close to free, you're just copying one value from the incoming request onto the outgoing one.
3.2 Asynchronous messages too

This is where a lot of implementations quietly fall short. It's easy to remember the header on a synchronous HTTP call and forget that a Kafka event, an SQS message, or any other async hop needs the same treatment. If the order service publishes an event and the id never makes it into the message, the chain snaps the moment anything picks that event up asynchronously.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352638-725392313.png
blocks.alt: A correlation id travels inside Kafka message headers, not just HTTP requests

blocks.title: Async is not optional
blocks.content: The moment your architecture has a queue or an event bus anywhere in the path, that hop needs the id attached to the message itself, usually in its headers or metadata, not buried inside a payload field where a consumer might not think to look.
3.3 Picking a header name
None of the common choices is objectively correct, they're just conventions different ecosystems settled on.

{"headers":["Header","Where you'll see it"],"rows":[["X-Correlation-ID","Widely used custom header, no formal standard behind it"],["X-Request-ID","Same idea, common in Rails influenced ecosystems"],["traceparent","The W3C Trace Context standard header, used by full tracing systems"]]}
Pick one, document it, and make sure every service your organization owns actually reads and writes that exact name.
4. Correlation id versus distributed tracing

If you've read about distributed tracing already, this should sound familiar, it's meant to. A correlation id is really a simpler, logging focused version of what a trace id does inside a full tracing system like Jaeger or Zipkin. Distributed tracing adds spans, parent child relationships between calls, and precise timing for each hop, on top of the same underlying idea of one id following a request around.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352638-361541331.png
blocks.alt: A correlation id ties log lines together, a trace id also ties spans and timing together

blocks.content: Because the core idea overlaps so much, a lot of real systems don't bother maintaining two separate ids. They just use the trace id as the correlation id, so the same value showing up in a tracing dashboard also shows up in every plain text log line.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["One id to search for across logs and traces","Needs a tracing SDK wired into every service upfront"],["No separate mapping step during an incident","Trace ids tend to be longer and clunkier to paste around"],["Less machinery to maintain overall","If a trace gets sampled out, you lose the shared id along with it"]]}
5. Implementation

Two problems need solving in code. Something has to generate or extract the id right when a request starts. And that id needs to be reachable from anywhere in the request's execution, your logging call, your outgoing HTTP client, some helper function three layers deep, without you manually threading it through every function signature in between.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352640-836807871.png
blocks.alt: Middleware runs first, checks for an existing id, generates one if missing

blocks.content: 5.1 Generating or extracting the id

A small piece of middleware, placed before everything else, checks the incoming request for the header. If it's already there, probably because an upstream service or the client itself set it, reuse it. If it's missing, this request is the first to arrive at your system, so generate a fresh one right here.
5.2 Carrying it without threading it everywhere
blocks.text: 5.2 Carrying it without threading it everywhere

blocks.content: Passing the id as a parameter into every function that might eventually need to log something would work, but it's miserable to maintain, every signature in your codebase ends up polluted with a value most of them don't actually care about. Node gives you a cleaner tool for this, AsyncLocalStorage, which behaves like a thread local variable except it follows the async call chain instead of an OS thread.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352641-570541632.png
blocks.alt: Async local storage carries the correlation id through a request without passing it as a parameter

blocks.title: Watch your async boundaries
blocks.content: AsyncLocalStorage follows promises and async/await just fine, but a callback that escapes the run context in an unusual way, an old callback based library, a raw event emitter, can lose the id. Test this against your actual stack before trusting it in production.
5.3 Using it in logs and outgoing calls
blocks.text: 5.3 Using it in logs and outgoing calls

blocks.content: Once the id lives in AsyncLocalStorage, your logger and your outgoing HTTP client can both reach into it without any function along the way needing to know it exists.
6. Worked example: a checkout request

A customer hits checkout. The request lands at the API gateway first, which doesn't find an X-Correlation-ID header on the incoming request, so it generates one, something like 8f14e45f, and attaches it going forward.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352641-16668946.png
blocks.alt: One correlation id follows a checkout request through cart, inventory, and payment services

blocks.content: ["Gateway generates 8f14e45f and forwards the request to the cart service.","Cart service logs 8f14e45f while validating the cart, then forwards it to inventory.","Inventory service logs 8f14e45f while reserving stock, then forwards it to payment.","Payment service logs 8f14e45f, attempts the charge, and this time the charge fails."]
items: Gateway generates 8f14e45f and forwards the request to the cart service.
Cart service logs 8f14e45f while validating the cart, then forwards it to inventory.
Inventory service logs 8f14e45f while reserving stock, then forwards it to payment.
Payment service logs 8f14e45f, attempts the charge, and this time the charge fails.

blocks.title: Sample log lines
blocks.text:
gateway: [8f14e45f] received checkout request for user 4821
cart: [8f14e45f] validated cart, 3 items, total 129.97
inventory: [8f14e45f] reserved stock for 3 items
payment: [8f14e45f] charge failed, card declined

blocks.content: An engineer gets paged. All they know at first is roughly when it happened and that one customer's checkout failed. They pull up the gateway logs, find the request, and grab its correlation id.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352642-242747862.png
blocks.alt: An engineer filters logs across every service by one correlation id during an incident

blocks.content: From there, one search, filter every service's logs for 8f14e45f, and the entire path lights up in order: cart validated fine, inventory reserved fine, payment threw a specific card declined error. Twenty minutes of grepping across five log files turns into one query.
7. The interview angle

This is a small detail, and that's exactly why it's worth mentioning. Anyone can draw boxes and arrows in a system design interview and say the cart service talks to the payment service. Far fewer candidates bring up how you'd actually debug that system at 3 AM when something breaks in production.
Bringing up correlation ids unprompted tells an interviewer you've actually operated a system like this, not just diagrammed one.

["Mention where the id gets generated, at the edge, not scattered across services","Mention the header name and that every service has to agree on it","Mention that it has to survive async hops too, not just synchronous calls","Mention how it's threaded through code without polluting every function signature"]

Mention the header name and that every service has to agree on it
Mention that it has to survive async hops too, not just synchronous calls
Mention how it's threaded through code without polluting every function signature

blocks.content: 8. Common gotchas

blocks.title: Forgetting async hops
blocks.content: The most common failure is remembering to forward the header on synchronous HTTP calls but forgetting it on a Kafka publish, an SQS send, or any other queue based hop. Audit every outbound integration, not just your REST calls.

blocks.title: Regenerating instead of forwarding
blocks.content: A service that generates its own new id instead of reusing the one it received breaks the chain from that point forward. Extract first, generate only as a fallback.

blocks.title: Inconsistent header names
blocks.content: If one team's service reads X-Request-ID and another reads X-Correlation-ID, they'll each dutifully generate their own id, and you end up with two disconnected ids instead of one, quietly defeating the whole point.
9. Key takeaway

A correlation id is one of the cheapest reliability investments you can make in a distributed system. Generate it once at the edge, forward it on every call it causes, synchronous or not, log it everywhere, and incidents that used to take twenty minutes of guesswork turn into one filtered search.

It won't replace full distributed tracing when you need a detailed timing breakdown across services, but it gets you most of the debugging value for a fraction of the setup cost, which is exactly why so many real systems still lean on it.
